title: Density

match.reason: Both bank points teach population density in geography (people per square kilometre), which is a different idea from the mass-per-volume density, displacement and floating taught by the new science point.

draft.title: Density
card: Density tells you how much mass is packed into a volume. Density = mass ÷ volume. It is often measured in g/cm³.
For example, 200 g of a material that takes up 50 cm³ has a density of 200 ÷ 50 = 4 g/cm³.
The volume of an irregular object can be found by displacement. Put it in water and measure how much the water level rises. That rise is the object's volume.
An object floats on a liquid if it is less dense than the liquid. It sinks if it is denser. Water has a density of about 1 g/cm³.
draft.remember: Density is mass ÷ volume. Less dense than the liquid means it floats.

a.q: A rock has a mass of 90 g and a volume of 30 cm³. What is its density?
opts: 3 g/cm³
0.33 g/cm³
60 g/cm³
120 g/cm³
a.why: Density = mass ÷ volume = 90 ÷ 30 = 3 g/cm³. Dividing volume by mass gives 0.33, which is the wrong way round.

b.q: Ana drops a lumpy stone into a measuring cylinder. The water rises from 40 mL to 55 mL, and the stone's mass is 30 g. Will it float in water?
opts: No, its density is 2 g/cm³, which is more than water
Yes, its density is 2 g/cm³, which is more than water
No, its density is 0.5 g/cm³, which is less than water
Yes, its density is 0.5 g/cm³, which is less than water
b.why: The volume is 55 - 40 = 15 mL, which is 15 cm³. Density = 30 ÷ 15 = 2 g/cm³. This is more than water's 1 g/cm³, so the stone sinks.
b.clue: The rise in water level is the stone's volume.

b.best: No, its density is 2 g/cm³, which is more than water

problems.detail: The question gives the water rise in mL, but the card only uses cm³ and never says that 1 mL = 1 cm³. Students need this fact to get an answer in g/cm³. It is explained only in the why. Add it to the card's displacement line.

check.summary: Both answers are correct (3 g/cm³; the stone sinks at 2 g/cm³). Question b relies on 1 mL = 1 cm³, which the card does not teach.
